cards.front: A portfolio's current credit risk is \(EL+UL=\)€50m. The calibrated §5.8 downturn (\(PD'=PD\cdot1{,}25\), \(LGD'=LGD\cdot1{,}05\)) reruns the IRB formula to a new credit risk of €64m. What makroökonomisches Risiko is added to the stack (in €)?

Problemfall, no full currency separation. FX Risikoposition (Corporates/Retail/LRG/CIU) = €40m; use the 15% Problemfall proxy for \(v_{fx}\); own-funds factor 8%. Compute the Fremdwährungs-Eigenmittelrisiko (in €).
Every quantified single risk (credit + market + op + CVA + participation + country + macro + Großkredite + FW-EM) sums to €100m. Compute the §5.10 sonstige-Risiken buffer (Puffer), in €.
Derive the Fremdwährungs-Eigenmittelrisiko for a €40m FX Risikoposition in the Problemfall with no full currency separation.

steps.prompt: With no full currency separation, what stands in for \(v_{fx}\) in the Problemfall?
steps.explain: When the data lacks a full currency split, the Leitfaden substitutes the scenario FX proxy: 15% in the Problemfall, 30% in the Extremfall.

steps.prompt: Compute the uplift to the assessment base \(\Delta\)Bemessungsgrundlage.
steps.explain: ΔBemessungsgrundlage = Risikoposition_FX · v_fx = 40m·0,15 = €6m of additional RWA base.

steps.prompt: Apply the own-funds factor to get the FW-EM-Risiko.
steps.explain: The 8% own-funds rate on the €6m base gives €0,48m of Deckungsmasse consumed. In the Extremfall this charge is €0 (not applied).

cards.front: The §5.8 downturn stresses the two credit drivers: \(PD'=PD\cdot\) {{c1}} and \(LGD'=LGD\cdot\) {{c2}}, calibrated (from the Leitfaden Stresstesting) to a ~{{c3}} GDP decline; the macro number is the difference covering both EL and UL.
Länderrisiko (§5.3) reuses the IRB engine but takes only the {{c1}} term, is computed {{c2}} collateral, uses the {{c3}} PD of the obligor's country, and excludes Ratingstufe {{c4}}.
The §5.9 Großkredite monitor relates the largest GvK exposures to {{c1}} (R-IPS members excluded), whereas the CRR Part Four legal large-exposure limit caps a single client/GvK at {{c2}} of {{c3}}.
Claim: 'The PD·1,25 / LGD·1,05 macro stress is a CRR-mandated calibration.' Classify the source spine and produce the tradeoff.
rubric: Names the calibration as an ÖRS modelling choice taken from the Leitfaden Stresstesting (a ~2% GDP decline → PDs +~25%, LGDs +~5%), NOT a CRR-forced number

States the tradeoff: a fixed point-in-time multiplier buys a simple, comparable downturn overlay across hundreds of banks, but cannot reflect each book's true PD/LGD cyclical sensitivity (a high-PD book actually moves more because the conditional-PD response is convex)
Notes the mechanic is reg-neutral: it reruns the same M5 IRB engine and differences EL+UL, so only the inputs are an ÖRS judgement

cards.front: An examiner asserts §5.9 Risiko aus Großkrediten IS the binding 25%-of-Tier-1 large-exposure rule. Classify (reg/ors/mixed) and produce the tradeoff.
rubric: Separates the layers: the 25%-of-Tier-1 cap on a single client/GvK is REG (CRR Part Four, binding legal limit); the §5.9 measure is an ÖRS sector-level concentration MONITOR relating aggregated largest GvK exposures to R-IPS CET1 (non-binding)

Produces the tradeoff: the legal limit is per-single-name and hard, so it misses aggregated sector build-up; the §5.9 monitor is macro-prudential and aggregate but non-binding, so it informs governance rather than capping anyone
Adds that concentration is also handled elsewhere — the HHI granularity add-on inside credit risk (M5) and internal limits — so §5.9 is one lens of three, not a substitute for the CRR limit

cards.front: Classify the Fremdwährungs-Eigenmittelrisiko charge: are the 8% factor AND its base reg or ÖRS? Produce the tradeoff.
rubric: Splits the construct: the 8% own-funds factor applied to the RWA-base uplift is REG (the CRR 8% own-funds rate); the base/scaling — the 3-yr FX vola or the 15% Problemfall / 30% Extremfall proxy, and the Problemfall-only application — is an ÖRS modelling choice

Produces the tradeoff: the 15%/30% proxy buys a usable number when full currency separation is missing, at the cost of crudeness (one flat vola across all FX books); the reg 8% keeps the charge anchored to the actual own-funds requirement
States the boundary: applying the 8%-on-RWA-base charge in the Extremfall is wrong — in a liquidation the capital-requirement effect is irrelevant, so it is a Problemfall-only construct

cards.front: Defend: why is makroökonomisches Risiko (§5.8) the one RTFA capital figure that includes EL, and why is it applied to credit risk only?

rubric.text: States it is the deliberate exception to the 'capital = pure UL' rule: it takes the difference in EL+UL because a downturn raises expected loss too, and the aim is the FULL credit-book deterioration
Explains it is credit-only because credit is the most material single risk; stressing the smaller risks would add complexity without materiality
Gives the mechanic: PD·1,25, LGD·1,05 (≈2% GDP decline), rerun the M5 IRB conditional-PD/K machinery, subtract the un-stressed total
Distinguishes it from M5's FX PD-elasticity (reacts to the exchange rate, not GDP)

antiPoints: Applying the PD·1,25 / LGD·1,05 stress to market or operational risk
Stripping EL out and taking only the UL difference
Claiming EL stays in the Deckungsmasse here as elsewhere
cards.modelAnswer: Makro risk breaks the usual 'capital number is pure UL, EL sits in the Deckungsmasse' rule on purpose: a cyclical downturn lifts expected loss as well as unexpected loss, so to capture the full deterioration of the book it differences EL+UL, not UL alone. It is applied to credit risk only because credit is the most material single risk — overlaying the same stress on the smaller risks would add complexity without materiality. Mechanically you stress the two drivers (PD·1,25, LGD·1,05, calibrated to a ~2% GDP decline from the Leitfaden Stresstesting), rerun the M5 IRB formula, and subtract the un-stressed credit total. It is distinct from M5's FX PD-elasticity, which reacts to the exchange rate rather than GDP.

cards.front: Defend the 5% sonstige-Risiken buffer (§5.10): what it stands for, how it scales, why a flat % is justified, and its weakness.

rubric.text: It is 5% of the SUM of all quantified risks → a ×1,05 on the whole stack, computed last on everything else (incl. macro and FW-EM); not a separate bolt-on line
It is a proxy for the qualitative §3.10 risks that are hard to model: strategic, reputational, business-model, systemic, model risk
Justified partly because future operating income is NOT counted in the Extremfall Deckungsmasse — the usual first cushion against soft risks is absent, so a flat capital buffer proxies it
Names the tradeoff: a flat % cannot distinguish a high- from a low-strategic/business-model-risk bank — comparability and simplicity bought at the cost of risk sensitivity

antiPoints: Calling it a CRR-mandated 5% (it is an ÖRS choice, not reg)
Treating it as a fixed independent line rather than 5% of the total
Computing it before the other §5 items so it understates the stack
cards.modelAnswer: The §5.10 buffer adds 5% of the sum of all quantified risks — a ×1,05 on the entire stack — and must be computed last, on everything else including the macro and FW-EM numbers, so it genuinely scales the whole total rather than being a separate line item. It stands in for the §3.10 qualitative risks (strategic, reputational, business-model, systemic, model) that are too soft to model directly. The flat-percentage approach is defensible chiefly because the Extremfall (a Liquidationsfall) Deckungsmasse excludes future operating income — the earnings stream that would normally be the first cushion against these risks — so a flat capital buffer is a reasonable proxy for that missing cushion. Its weakness is risk-insensitivity: it charges a bank with high strategic/business-model risk exactly the same 5% as a low-risk one, buying comparability across hundreds of banks at the cost of discrimination.

cards.front: Defend the separation of the Fremdwährungs-Eigenmittelrisiko (§5.10) from the FX credit-risk add-on (M5), including scenario applicability and mechanics.

rubric.text: FW-Eigenmittelrisiko hits the CAPITAL-REQUIREMENT side: FX appreciation → higher euro Saldo → higher Bemessungsgrundlage/RWA base → higher own-funds requirement → less free Deckungsmasse
The M5 FX credit add-on hits the EXPOSURE/LOSS side: appreciation raises the euro exposure/loss of FX loans → bigger UL

Scenario split: FW-EM is Problemfall ONLY (irrelevant in an Extremfall liquidation); the M5 FX credit add-on applies in BOTH scenarios; charging both is correct, charging FW-EM in the Extremfall is not
Mechanics of FW-EM: scale the Corporates/Retail/LRG/CIU FX Risikoposition by the 3-yr FX vola (or 15%/30% proxy), then take 8%

antiPoints: Treating the two FX effects as identical / intentional double-count
Applying the FW-Eigenmittelrisiko in the Extremfall
Saying FW-EM raises the exposure/loss rather than the capital-requirement base
cards.modelAnswer: These are two distinct FX effects. The FW-Eigenmittelrisiko works on the capital-requirement side: an FX appreciation raises the euro Saldo of FX loans, which lifts the Bemessungsgrundlage (RWA base) and hence the own-funds requirement, leaving less free Deckungsmasse. The M5 FX credit-risk add-on works on the asset side: the same appreciation raises the euro exposure and loss of FX loans, producing a bigger unexpected loss. They apply in different scenarios — the M5 add-on in both, the FW-Eigenmittelrisiko in the Problemfall only, because in an Extremfall liquidation the going-concern capital-requirement effect is irrelevant. Charging both in the Problemfall is correct; charging the FW-EM in the Extremfall is the error. Mechanically the FW-EM scales the Corporates/Retail/LRG/CIU FX Risikoposition by the 3-yr FX vola (or the 15%/30% proxy when currency separation is missing) and takes 8% of that base.
